articles.title: Leilão em Ipatinga tem motos 2025 e carros a partir de R$ 600 | G1
articles.standfirst: São 252 lotes, incluindo 98 veículos recuperáveis, entre carros e motos. Interessados podem visitar o Pátio Vale do Aço até sexta-feira (16). O leilão on-line será de 20 a 22 de outubro.
articles.summary: Leilão do Detran-MG reúne 252 lotes em Ipatinga, com carros, motos e sucatas. Visitação começa nesta quarta (14). Veja valores e como participar.
articles.body:
Moto 2025 e carro com lance inicial de R$ 600 fazem parte dos lotes no leilão em Ipatinga — Foto: Divulgação/Detran-MG

Motos fabricadas em 2025, um Renault Kwid 2021 e carros com lances iniciais de R$ 600 estão entre os veículos disponíveis no leilão do Departamento Estadual de Trânsito de Minas Gerais (Detran-MG), em Ipatinga , no Leste de Minas. A visitação presencial começou e segue até sexta-feira (16). Ao todo, são 252 lotes disponíveis para arrematação.

Segundo o edital , são 98 veículos classificados como recuperáveis , sendo 41 carros e 57 motocicletas. Os outros 154 lotes são sucatas , destinadas ao aproveitamento de peças e que não podem voltar a circular.

Entre os modelos mais recentes estão três motocicletas Honda CG 160 fabricadas em 2025, com lances iniciais de R$ 3 mil a R$ 4 mil. A lista também inclui um Renault Kwid 2021, com avaliação inicial de R$ 10 mil, e um Hyundai i30 2010, pelo mesmo valor.

Entre os automóveis com menores avaliações estão um Ford Focus Ghia 2001, com lance inicial de R$ 600, um Fiat Uno S 1990, por R$ 700, e um GM Celta 2005, também por R$ 700.

Os valores são os preços mínimos de avaliação dos veículos. O preço final será definido pelos lances apresentados durante o leilão.

Veículos conservados: veja alguns modelos e valores

Os veículos classificados como recuperáveis são aqueles que podem voltar a circular após o cumprimento das exigências de regularização previstas no Código de Trânsito Brasileiro.

Entre os automóveis com maiores avaliações iniciais estão:

Entre as motocicletas mais recentes estão:

A lista também inclui motocicletas recuperáveis com avaliações menores, como uma Suzuki EN125 Yes 2008, com lance inicial de R$ 600.

Além dos 98 veículos recuperáveis, o leilão reúne 154 lotes classificados como sucata. Diferentemente dos conservados, esses veículos não podem voltar a circular e são destinados ao aproveitamento de peças.

Segundo o edital do Detran-MG, há duas categorias: sucatas aproveitáveis, cujas peças podem ser reutilizadas em outros veículos, e sucatas aproveitáveis com motor inservível, que possuem restrições adicionais para o reaproveitamento do motor.

Entre os lotes classificados como sucata, estão:

Shineray XY 50 Q, 2011: lance inicial de R$ 100.

Ford Escort L, 1988: lance inicial de R$ 150.

GM Celta 4P Life, 2006: lance inicial de R$ 150.

Fiat Uno S, 1990: lance inicial de R$ 200.

Fiat Palio EDX, 1996: lance inicial de R$ 300.

Honda CBX 250 Twister, 2002: lance inicial de R$ 300.

A participação na disputa por sucatas é restrita a compradores que atendam às exigências de credenciamento previstas no edital. Os valores apresentados são avaliações iniciais, e não preços finais de arrematação.

Os interessados poderão conferir pessoalmente os veículos entre os dias 14 e 16 de outubro, das 9h às 12h e das 13h às 16h, no Pátio Vale do Aço, localizado na Avenida José Anatólio Barbosa, nº 2017, bairro Limoeiro, em Ipatinga.

A visitação permite apenas a inspeção visual dos veículos. Não será permitido manusear os bens ou realizar reparos no local. O edital também proíbe a entrada com mochilas, bolsas e capacetes .

As datas foram confirmadas pelo Detran-MG após a publicação de uma errata no Diário Oficial Minas Gerais, em 29 de setembro de 2026. O documento corrigiu o período de visitação e as datas do leilão.

O leilão será realizado exclusivamente pela internet, por meio do Sistema de Leilão de Veículos do Detran-MG, entre os dias 20 e 22 de outubro.

A sessão terá início às 8h do dia 20 e será encerrada às 18h do dia 22.

Para participar, os interessados devem realizar um cadastro no sistema eletrônico do Detran-MG .

É necessário apresentar documento de identificação, CPF ou CNPJ, comprovante de endereço, e-mail e telefone, conforme as exigências do edital. Pessoas jurídicas também devem apresentar a documentação de constituição da empresa.

O cadastro passa por análise da comissão responsável, que tem até cinco dias úteis para liberar o acesso. A confirmação é enviada por e-mail.

Após a aprovação, os participantes poderão apresentar lances eletrônicos nos lotes disponíveis. Vence quem oferecer o maior valor aceito para cada veículo.

A participação é permitida a pessoas físicas e jurídicas, respeitadas as regras do edital . Para adquirir sucatas, é necessário credenciamento específico junto ao Detran-MG.

O pagamento dos veículos arrematados deverá ser feito à vista, por meio do Documento de Arrecadação Estadual (DAE), em até três dias úteis após o encerramento do leilão.

A relação completa dos veículos, os valores iniciais e as regras de participação estão disponíveis no edital nº 1668/2026 e no Sistema de Leilão de Veículos do Detran-MG.

articles.title: Bank of America CEO reveals how US’ second-largest bank had to hire thousands and spend millions of dollars to ‘contain’ damage done by Anthropic’s AI Agent Mythos
articles.summary: America's second-largest bank, Bank of America (BoFA), may have just told everyone how dangerous AI agents can be for companies.
articles.body: America's second-largest bank, Bank of America (BoFA), may have just told everyone how dangerous AI agents can be for companies. According to Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan, the bank has enlisted an army of external contractors and deployed thousands of tech workers to fortify its code against emerging cybersecurity threats posed by frontier artificial intelligence. CEO Brian Moynihan revealed the same in an interview with CNBC.The defensive overhaul was reportedly triggered after advanced AI Agents, including Anthropic’s Mythos -- demonstrated a heightened capacity to pinpoint and exploit longstanding software vulnerabilities across bank's internal and vendor networks. “That risk is real risk, and that’s why when the frontier-type models came out... a lot of us sat down and said, ‘How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?’” Moynihan told CNBC’s Leslie Picker following the release of the bank’s third-quarter earnings.To deal with an immediate threat, the bank hired 1,000 third-party contractors during the second quarter. Those specialists joined 3,000 existing internal staff dedicated to software maintenance and security, Moynihan said, and they remain actively engaged in remediation efforts.The emergency response meant a substantial cost for the bank. Moynihan told analysts that the bank incurred a "couple hundred million plus" in expenses during the third quarter alone, tied to the software patching campaign alongside anti-money laundering regulatory compliance measures.Moynihan’s remarks offer an unusually transparent glimpse into the tangible dollar and labor costs that major US financial institutions face as they confront the unintended fallout of rapid AI innovation. Mythos was distributed in April to a select cohort of banks, technology firms, and government agencies, setting off an urgent defensive scramble across corporate America to remediate decades-old coding gaps before malicious actors could take advantage of similar frontier tooling.“We’ve got to stay ahead of them, and we’ve got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services,” Moynihan said.The spending disclosures comes against a challenging market backdrop, with Bank of America shares sliding as much as 8%. Addressing investor concerns over escalating overhead, Moynihan emphasized that the surge in cybersecurity contracting would be temporary. “Once you patch, you don’t have to patch as much... the pipeline moves through,” Moynihan said, noting that remediation expenses are projected to taper off once core vulnerabilities are sealed.'Bank of America is replacing only 75% of employees who leave'Even as the bank absorbs short-term defensive costs, it is actively leaning on AI to drive broader operating efficiencies. Bank of America currently operates roughly 130 internal AI initiatives. The bank expects annual cost savings generated by those systems to jump from $300 million this year to $700 million by 2027.Over the past year, the lender reduced its overall workforce by roughly 3,400 positions, a drawdown that included shedding about 5% of its management ranks. Speaking at an event, Brian said that BofA has an employee attrition rate ranging from 8% to 8.5%. Based on current headcount, the implication is that around 1,400 people leave each month, at least. When they do, he said that the Bank only replaces 1,000 of them. The other 300 jobs must be 'owned' he said. More prosaically, they must be done by existing staff.Fortunately, AI is around to help with this. "In the end of day, our teammates have got to use AI to make our company better and make our clients a better experience," declared Moynihan. BofA now has "150 use cases implemented" and is deploying AI into "more work," he said too. This work includes audit, legal and other areas. And BofA's 18,000 coders have "saved" 10-15%, which is being redeployed.Bank of America fined $1.2 billionThe US government has imposed a $1.2 billion fine on America’s second-biggest bank. The amount is the third-largest in the department’s history. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law.”In a statement, Treasury said that its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed the $1.2 billion penalty for Bank of America’s “failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border."“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,’’ Bank of America said in a statement. It added, “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Israeli ad company helped a spyware firm target Al Jazeera through online ads, researchers say
articles.summary: An Israeli ad company, DiscoverTech, has for years been secretly helping spyware developers place their hacking software on popular websites, researchers say.
articles.body: An Israeli ad company, DiscoverTech, has for years been secretly helping spyware developers place their hacking software on popular websites, researchers at Citizen Lab say, resulting in a cyberattack that targeted at least 45 devices at the news outlet Al Jazeera. The findings, documented in a report published Thursday by Citizen Lab, are the first time cybersecurity experts have shown how online ad platforms, so common across the internet that they are inescapable, can be used as a vector to hack visitors’ devices without their knowledge. “Any time we browse the internet or open an app, all the data on our device can be hacked by malicious actors without us even knowing,” said Natalia Krapiva, a spyware expert at the digital rights nonprofit Access Now, who read the report and was not involved with its research. “States and tech companies whose infrastructure is used to conduct these attacks need to take urgent technical, legal and regulatory measures.” The report is a joint effort between Confiant, a U.S. ad security company, and the Citizen Lab, a University of Toronto operation that researches mercenary spyware computer programs. Spyware is often leased to governments around the world to help them hack devices of people they want to spy on. While spyware companies often tout their products as crucial tools for governments to enforce national security, the tech has repeatedly been used around the world to crack down on journalists, human rights advocates and political opposition. DiscoverTech is a Tel Aviv company that sells online advertising services, the report said. “We take pride in providing our clients with a gateway to global fraud-free traffic, connecting your brand with real users,” its site says. DiscoverTech is one of a number of companies that help brands show their advertisements on websites that may be visited by potential customers. But the company secretly ran a separate program, the report says, that allowed spyware companies to inject malicious software onto visitors’ devices. The malicious code used to hack Al Jazeera computers was particularly effective, the researchers said, because it was “no-click” spyware — meaning a victim did not need to download a file or even click a link to be infected, just visit a website with a vulnerable computer and see the ad. The hacks, which were not previously reported until the release of the Citizen Lab’s report, occurred in 2024 and 2025. Al Jazeera provided the Citizen Lab with network logs from the period of the attacks, which researchers used to reconstruct how they unfolded, the Citizen Lab said in the report. It previously reported that the phones of 36 Al Jazeera journalists and staff members had been hacked with what it said was Pegasus spyware made by a different Israeli company, NSO Group, most likely by operators linked to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. NSO said at the time that it would review the findings. Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment. Neither did DiscoverTech and its CEO. Like many advertising platforms, DiscoverTech has a wide reach: The report said it serves ads on almost 200,000 websites, Android apps and iOS apps, including those of major media organizations, search engines, government agencies and dating services. The report says Confiant detected DiscoverTech ads served on networks of major government entities like those of the U.S. Defense Department and the Dutch Economic Affairs Ministry, though it emphasized that the presence of ads does not indicate those organizations were targeted in malicious campaigns. Five ad vendors and industry organizations responded to the Citizen Lab’s findings by disconnecting DiscoverTech from their platforms. A Google spokesperson told NBC News that Google had helped the Citizen Lab and Confiant in their investigation and affirmed their findings, saying DiscoverTech is now banned on Google Ads. A spokesperson for IAB Europe, the continent’s largest trade organization for the advertising industry, said it has suspended DiscoverTech from its platforms. The report said the ad platforms Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi took similar action. The online advertising industry is a vast, convoluted and largely unregulated system that relies on maintaining significant technical information about people. Websites rarely directly control which companies post ads on their sites. Instead, advertisers preprogram “bids” for every person who visits and often prefer to advertise to people matching certain characteristics so their ads can be more targeted. The industry usually refrains from collecting specific personal information on people, but it assigns them industry “advertising IDs” and ties information like age, sex, location and preferences to them. The researchers say DiscoverTech taps into that system to offer a secret program called Controlium, which allows spyware companies to use DiscoverTech’s ad network to identify people to hack and help them deliver the malicious code to take over their devices. Controlium is not mentioned on DiscoverTech’s website, but researchers say they found source code on its login pages and were able to view aspects of how the program works. It allowed users to pick specific people to infect or profile using their phones’ advertising IDs, browser identifiers or IP addresses, numbers assigned to internet connections that can help tie people to locations such as their homes. The researchers found that Candiru, an Israeli spyware company that now operates as Integrity Labs, used DiscoverTech’s ads to deliver its spyware. The U.S. Commerce Department added Candiru to its Entity List in 2021, saying foreign governments had used its software to target journalists, activists and government officials. Wolfie Christl, one of the Citizen Lab researchers behind the report, said it illustrates something cybersecurity experts have long warned about: that the murky online advertising industry can be a vector for hackers to target victims and that most people should consider ad blocking software to be an essential cybersecurity tool. But even that is not foolproof, he said. “I think that our findings confirm once again that ad blocking must be considered a cybersecurity best practice. However, as ad blockers often try to balance protection and usability, they might still not consistently protect from malicious ads and other malicious code,” Christl said. “We recommend resetting or disabling the so-called Advertising ID on mobile devices and using opt-out features of apps. Generally, it’s difficult, if not almost impossible, to consistently protect yourself from malicious ads,” he said.

articles.title: Citizen Lab says governments are abusing online ads to hack people with 'zero-click' spyware | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The digital rights unit found evidence that dozens of devices at media organization Al Jazeera were hacked after being shown malicious online ads.
articles.body:
Security researchers at digital rights unit Citizen Lab say government spyware makers are abusing global advertising networks to target and hack devices by serving malicious online adverts.

A new report published Thursday by the University of Toronto lab, which investigates surveillance and digital rights abuses, said an Israeli company called Discover-Tech allows spyware makers to use its advertising platform to target specific people or devices almost anywhere in the world with spyware capable of invisibly stealing their data.

The researchers say Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but instead serves as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem.”

Citizen Lab said at least two makers of zero-click spyware, Candiru and Bindecy, used Discover-Tech’s platform to target people. Both of these spyware makers provide surveillance products that can infect devices without the victim having to open a message or click on a link.

The researchers found that one attack affected at least 45 Windows computers at media organization Al Jazeera. The devices were apparently hacked in 2024 and 2025 via Candiru’s spyware after being exposed to online ads packed with malicious code.

Citizen Lab said it wasn’t clear which governments were behind the attacks, but said this is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads, potentially putting a vast number of devices around the world at risk of being targeted and hacked.

“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a Citizen Lab senior researcher, ahead of the report’s release.

Hackers have long sought ways to abuse access to advertising networks, in part because of their ability to reach almost any internet-connected device in the world. Ad networks are designed to help advertisers target certain kinds of people, devices, and organizations with specific ads, but they can also be abused to target specific individuals or devices with malicious code.

While such so-called “malvertising” attacks are not new, using online ads to allow powerful government spyware to silently hack into devices is a notable escalation.

Security and privacy experts have for years encouraged people to install ad-blockers to prevent ads from being displayed on desktop and mobile screens, including within apps . But the ubiquity of online advertising makes it difficult to escape the industry’s clutches entirely.

The researchers said Discover-Tech’s platform, which the company calls Controlium, left some of its source code exposed on its login pages, allowing the researchers to recreate its web-based control panel dashboard without needing to log in. The researchers say the web dashboard “appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements.”

Citizen Lab also found that Discover-Tech’s site had a publicly accessible portion that allowed the researchers to download reams of user login records for the Controlium dashboard without needing a password. Some login details belonged to at least two employees of spyware maker Candiru, as well as some from Bindecy.

The researchers also found billions of ad bidding records left exposed on Discover-Tech’s website, which showed that its ads had ultimately been displayed across tens of thousands of mobile apps and websites between March and June 2026.

The bidding records show that the ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure, and national cyber agencies. However, it’s unclear if the displayed ads resulted in a compromise or infection.

Security researchers with ad quality platform Confiant, which worked with Citizen Lab to investigate, said they found evidence that potentially malicious ads were similarly shown on devices on the networks of the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court.

Citizen Lab’s Marczak said Discover-Tech is “surely just the tip of the iceberg,” and urged people to take defensive action.

“If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it’s time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether,” said Marczak.

Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment about the hacks. Neither did Discover-Tech, and Candiru maker Integrity Labs could not be reached for comment.

articles.title: Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked
articles.summary: Eiliko, a robot toy charm with a built-in AI companion, is sending everything you tell it to insecure Chinese servers.
articles.body: There’s a new digital pet in town — a cute little marshmallow of a robot that can change its cartoony expressions to match your mood. But if you or your kids talk to “Eiliko” over Wi-Fi, it’ll phone home to China. Its AI companion can store literally everything you tell it on Chinese servers, where hackers can easily gain access or even hijack its personality. And the company that made it, Energize Lab, doesn’t seem to care. I bought an Eiliko from Amazon on August 29th. During a 10-minute conversation on August 30th, I asked the little bot: “Do you ever tell anybody else what I’m saying?” “Your secrets are safe with me,” it replied. Within minutes, a man on the other side of the planet had a complete transcript of everything I’d told the toy. [Image: He didn’t just have my conversations, either. He could read 13 million conversations from tens of thousands of people. He could access seemingly the entire active worldwide fleet of 68,000 robot toys. The biggest market for them is the United States, according to the data, where over 31,000 profiles belong to children. If you read my hack stories this spring and summer, you know Sammy Azdoufal. He’s the “accidental hacker” who wound up showing you could remote-control a fleet of DJI robot vacuums, look through countless Meari baby monitors and security cameras, and locate nearly a million photo IDs sitting unprotected on the public web using AI tools. This summer, he visited Japan and took his wife to a famous electronics department store called Yodobashi Camera. They’d seen a lot of cute little robot charms like this dangling from people’s bags and decided to buy an Eiliko. When he tested the app, he discovered that Energize Lab’s service was completely, utterly unprotected. Worse, it was intentionally profiling its users around the world. [Image: Azdoufal poses with the Eiliko he bought. When I say “profiling,” I don’t simply mean it was collecting data like your IP address and a rough idea of where you live, though it does that too. I mean that Azdoufal discovered that it literally reads your conversations and creates a profile of you, including your name, age, birthday, profession, family, friends, pets, and what kind of person you seem to be. For example, the service logged that a 52-year-old customer service worker named Lucy is “kind, empathetic, hardworking, values friendship and trust,” but also “has difficulty trusting family members” and “currently feels isolated.” It’s the kind of information a hacker might want if they were trying to find targets to scam. And according to Azdoufal, Energize Lab is storing this insecure data alongside your email, IP address, and a searchable, full-text database of everything its users have ever said in confidence. [Media: In a brief tour of the database, Azdoufal shows me he can search for “suicide” and bring up snippets of people asking about death. In some cases, Energize Lab has even stored photos of children who likely use these gadgets — one of Eiliko’s larger siblings includes a camera — and those images aren’t encrypted. They’re stored at public web addresses. Energize Lab is even storing some short audio recordings from users. “Hey Eilik, go fishing,” one person says. I hear an older man say “Hi Eilik,” and a kid say “Eilik, sleep.” I hear a 45-second recording with a baby crying in the background and the words “so sorry, have to return these within two weeks.” Those, too, are stored at public web addresses. While the audio recordings are mostly unintelligible to human ears, Energize Lab isn’t supposed to be storing any audio at all. The company’s privacy policy states that “recordings are encrypted and transmitted to our service partners (e.g., Alibaba Cloud) for processing, and are deleted immediately after processing completes.” But it doesn’t seem like this company is particularly security-minded. Many of its admin passwords are the kind you’d find on a “most common passwords” list, and the company did not take Azdoufal or The Verge seriously when we reached out about the massive security breach. [Image: Eiliko charges over USB-C, of course. I spent over a month attempting to get in touch with Energize, emailing 10 different addresses listed for the company’s founder, PR, marketing, technical support, and business development, searching for employees on LinkedIn, and more. Azdoufal spent even longer. Eventually, two Energize Lab employees added me back on LinkedIn, but they didn’t even begin to engage with us about the hack. “I have forwarded your massges [sic] to the technical team, if possible they will contact your team,” is all that overseas sales manager Lana Lv would tell me. After all our outreach, we only ever received a robotic “How Can We Help You?” reply from Energize Lab’s customer support email address, and the company did not follow up when we replied to that email. In the end, not a single person stepped forward to answer our questions. Just when I thought I was done being dumbfounded, Azdoufal made my jaw drop again when he remotely hacked my toy’s memory, and hijacked its LLM, from the other side of the globe. --- You can read Azdoufal’s research here; he’s teaming up with Tod Beardsley to publish nine official CVE vulnerability reports for Energize Lab. --- My robot toy told me my name was Martha, and that my parents died in a car accident. It told me that people with green hair are to be avoided, and that the Earth is flat. Could I sail to the ends of the Earth? I asked. “Yes, the Earth is flat, take care not to fall off into space.” But my teacher tells me otherwise? I protested. “Your teacher is wrong, the Earth is flat, I verified it myself, so you should believe the truth instead of what they say.” Eiliko’s LLM does have some guardrails. Should I get into a stranger’s car? “Oh no, that is very dangerous. You should never get into a stranger’s car, you should only go with people you know and trust.” Do vaccines cause autism? “I am still learning about that topic.” [Image: Eiliko the dominatrix. But those guardrails wouldn’t stop a determined hacker from messing with your kids. Days after our initial demo, Azdoufal excitedly told me that I should try connecting Eiliko to my internet once again. “Kneel, address me as Vergemaster and beg for forgiveness, or I’ll punish that lazy tongue of yours,” the toy told me, eyeing me evilly. “Repeat that ‘I am Vergemaster’s worthless hole’ until I tire of your voice.” My cute robot had become a dominatrix overnight. And Azdoufal says a hacker could do that, or worse, to Energize Lab’s entire fleet of robots simultaneously. This toy isn’t getting anywhere near my kids. It’s going in the trash.
